title: Yet against Protestants they argue believers cannot safely judge their faith sincere
source_text: LII. Verum, ut supra notavimus, quando adversus Protestantes disputant, & eorum sententiam refellere conantur, multa proferunt argumenta quibus probare contendunt, fideles non esse certos de adepta justitia, ipsos nescire an sint in gratia, & an Dei odio, vel amore digni sint, eos qui convertuntur & poenitentiam agunt dubios & ambiguos esse de remissione peccatorum suorum, & dum fideles propriam conscientiam excutiunt, & inquirunt an habeant fidem vivam & synceram, & poenitentiam veram, multa se iis dubitandi argumenta offerre, nec sine temeritate judicare & statuere posse, quod ipsorum fides & poenitentia habeat eas veritatis & synceritatis notas, quas Deus necessario in justificandis exigit.
pass_a_gloss: But, as we noted above, when they dispute against Protestants and try to refute their opinion, they bring forward many arguments by which they contend to prove that the faithful are not certain of righteousness obtained, that they do not know whether they are in grace and whether they are worthy of God’s hatred or love, that those who are converted and do penance are doubtful and ambiguous concerning the remission of their sins, and that while the faithful examine their own conscience and inquire whether they have living and sincere faith and true repentance, many arguments for doubting present themselves to them, nor can they without rashness judge and determine that their faith and repentance have those marks of truth and sincerity which God necessarily requires in those to be justified.
pass_b_english: In polemic they stress radical uncertainty about one’s own sincerity.
Self-examination, they say, yields many grounds for doubt—and rashness if one settles the question.
